newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to host Mideast summit without Mubarak.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to host Mideast summit without Mubarak.

text.p: Despite Arab pleas for a delay and a polite decline from Egypt, President Bill Clinton will open a Middle East crisis summit on Tuesday with leaders of Israel, the Palestinians and Jordan, the White House said on Monday.

Although Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak -- a key voice for moderate Arabs -- declined to attend the hastily called two-day summit, Clinton decided to press ahead with talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the discussions, which were prompted by Israeli-Palestinian violence that threatened to derail the whole Middle East peace process, would focus on several key questions:
"How can we restore calm? What can we do to bring an end to the violence? How can we re-engage the (peace) process?"

Clinton was expected to meet with King Hussein at the White House on Monday night, and hold private talks on Tuesday morning with Netanyahu and Arafat. That would be followed by a general session with all the participants.
Those meetings were all scheduled to take place in the White House, but the venue for Wednesday's talks remained open depending on how things proceeded, officials said.
The State Department said Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa would come to Washington for the summit but would not take a direct part in the talks.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said Moussa would merely be "available for consultations with the parties ... That is the choice of the Egyptian government."

Arafat and Mubarak, who met in Egypt on Monday before Arafat travelled to Europe and Washington, had wanted to postpone the summit pending assurances it would bring firm guarantees of Israeli gestures toward the Palestinians.

But McCurry told reporters: "We attached no preconditions to the discussions but we asked only that the leaders arrive only in a frame of mind to address the fundamental questions that will be before them."
"We are not excluding items from consideration for this conference," he said. "We fully expect all sides to bring the issues up that are relevant."

The summit takes place not only against a backdrop of a sudden resumption of Israeli-Palestinian violence but in the midst of the U.S. election campaign, with Clinton under challenge by Republican Bob Dole in the Nov. 5 balloting.
Fighting erupted in the West Bank and Gaza last week after Israel opened a pedestrian tunnel to archaeological sites by Jerusalem's Temple Mount, sacred to both Judaism and Islam.
Fifty-five Palestinians and 14 Israelis were killed in five days of clashes.

"It's clear to me that the Middle East peace process is in a state of crisis," Secretary of State Warren Christopher said. "The president took an extraordinary step in inviting the parties to come here to Washington for these meetings."
But Christopher sought to play down chances for a major breakthrough at the Washington talks.
"I think we ought to recognise the limitations," he said before talks with Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus. "The parties are quite estranged and raw because of the violence and killings."

He described the basic aims of the summit as "first that the parties will begin to talk together again, second that they will commit to end the violence, and third that they will find the basis for resuming negotiations."
Despite the pressures of his re-election campaign schedule, including a televised debate with Dole next Sunday night, Clinton cleared his calendar through the middle of the week to act as mediator.

One of the highlights of his presidency was his shepherding of Arafat and the late Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin into a "historic handshake" at 1993 White House ceremonies in which Israel and the Palestinians signed a peace accord designed to end a long and bloody feud.
